specStatements.text: Distance is how far an object moves. Distance does not involve direction. Distance is a scalar quantity.

Displacement includes both the distance an object moves, measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point and the direction of that straight line. Displacement is a vector quantity.
Students should be able to express a displacement in terms of both the magnitude and direction.
Speed does not involve direction. Speed is a scalar quantity.
The speed of a moving object is rarely constant. When people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including: age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled.
Typical values may be taken as:
walking ̴ 1.5 m/s
running ̴ 3 m/s
cycling ̴ 6 m/s.
Students should be able to recall typical values of speed for a person walking, running and cycling as well as the typical values of speed for different types of transportation systems.
It is not only moving objects that have varying speed. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
Students should be able to make measurements of distance and time and then calculate speed s of objects.
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using the equation:
distance travelled = speed × time
[s = v t]
distance, s, in metres, m
speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
time, t, in seconds, s
Students should be able to calculate average speed for non-uniform motion.
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction. Velocity is a vector quantity.
Students should be able to explain the vector–scalar distinction as it applies to displacement, distance, velocity and speed.
(HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively, with examples, that motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity.
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance–time graph.
The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance–time graph.
(HT only) If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent and measuring the gradient of the distance–time graph at that time.

Students should be able to draw distance–time graphs from measurements and extract and interpret lines and slopes of distance–time graphs, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
Students should be able to determine speed from a distance–time graph.
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using the equation:
acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken)
acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2
change in velocity, ∆ v, in metres per second, m/s
time, t, in seconds, s
An object that slows down is decelerating.
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations.
The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
(HT only) The distance travelled by an object (or displacement of an object) can be calculated from the area under a velocity–time graph.
Students should be able to:
• draw velocity–time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration
• (HT only) interpret enclosed areas in velocity–time graphs to determine distance travelled (or displacement)
• (HT only) measure, when appropriate, the area under a velocity–time graph by counting squares.
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration:
(final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance
final velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s
initial velocity, u, in metres per second, m/s
acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2
distance, s, in metres, m
Near the Earth’s surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.
An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. Eventually the resultant force will be zero and the object will move at its terminal velocity.
(Physics only) Students should be able to:
• draw and interpret velocity–time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity
• interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

concepts.definition: Distance is how far an object moves. It is measured along the whole path the object actually travels, and it does not involve direction. Distance is therefore a scalar quantity: it is fully described by a magnitude and a unit, for example 400 m.

Displacement includes both the distance an object moves, measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point, and the direction of that straight line. Displacement is a vector quantity. Because it is measured start-to-finish in a straight line, the magnitude of the displacement can never be greater than the distance travelled, and it is zero whenever an object returns to its starting point.

A displacement is only fully stated when both parts are given: the magnitude (a number and a unit) and the direction of the straight line from start point to finish point. '250 m' is not a displacement; '250 m due north' is. The direction is that of the straight line from start to finish, not the direction the object happened to be moving in at the end.
Speed tells you how quickly an object moves but does not involve direction, so speed is a scalar quantity. Speed is measured in metres per second, m/s.

The speed of a moving object is rarely constant. When people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing - they start, stop, slow for corners and speed up again. A single quoted speed for a whole journey is therefore normally an average rather than a value held at every instant.

The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled. Terrain matters because rough or steep ground slows a person down; distance travelled matters because a speed that can be held over 100 m cannot be held over 10 km.

Typical values may be taken as: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. These are approximate values to be recalled and used in estimates; they are not fixed constants, because real speeds vary from person to person and journey to journey.

Students are expected to recall typical speeds for different types of transportation system as well as for people. Values in common use are about 25 m/s for a car, about 55 m/s for a train and about 250 m/s for a passenger aeroplane. Like the values for walking, running and cycling, these are approximate figures for estimating, and the specification itself only fixes the values for walking, running, cycling and the speed of sound.

concepts.term: Varying speeds of sound and wind
concepts.definition: It is not only moving objects that have varying speed. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary. The speed of sound depends on the medium and on its conditions, and wind speed changes from moment to moment, so any quoted figure is a typical value.

concepts.term: Typical speed of sound in air
concepts.definition: A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. This is the figure to use in calculations such as echo and thunder problems unless a question supplies a different value.

Speed is found by measuring a distance and the time taken to travel it, then dividing the distance by the time. The distance is measured with a suitable instrument such as a metre rule, tape measure or trundle wheel, and the time with a stopwatch or light gates; both measurements must be in the base units, metres and seconds, before dividing.

concepts.term: The equation distance travelled = speed × time
concepts.definition: For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using the equation distance travelled = speed × time, written in symbols as s = v t, where distance, s, is in metres, m; speed, v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s. This equation must be recalled. Times given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before it is used.

Real motion is non-uniform, so the useful quantity is average speed: the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey, including any time spent stationary. It is not the mean of the separate speeds of the different parts of a journey, and it is not the speed of any one part.

The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction. Velocity is a vector quantity, so a velocity is only fully stated when a magnitude and a direction are both given, for example 12 m/s due east.

Distance and speed are scalars: they have magnitude only. Displacement and velocity are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. Each vector is the directional partner of a scalar - displacement is the vector partner of distance, and velocity is the vector partner of speed.

(HT only) An object moving in a circle can have a constant speed while its velocity changes continuously, because the direction of motion changes at every point around the circle. Since velocity is a vector, a change of direction alone is a change of velocity. Examples include a car going round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s, a planet in a near-circular orbit, and a ball whirled on a string.

If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance-time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis. A horizontal line means the object is stationary, because the distance is not changing while time passes; a straight sloping line means constant speed; a curve means the speed is changing.

concepts.term: Speed from the gradient of a distance-time graph
concepts.definition: The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph. The gradient is found by taking a triangle on the line and dividing the change in distance (in m) by the change in time (in s), giving a speed in m/s. A steeper line means a greater speed.

concepts.term: Tangent to a curved distance-time graph
concepts.definition: (HT only) If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent and measuring the gradient of the distance-time graph at that time. The tangent is a straight line touching the curve at that one point; its gradient gives the speed at that instant, which is not the same as the average speed over the journey so far.

Measurements of distance and time are plotted as points and a line of best fit drawn; information is then read back off the graph. Interpreting the graph means translating between graphical and numerical form: identifying stationary sections, comparing speeds from the steepness of the lines, and calculating a speed from a slope.

The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using the equation acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), written in symbols as a = (∆v)/t, where acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s²; change in velocity, ∆v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s. This equation must be recalled. The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, not simply the final velocity.

An object that slows down is decelerating. Its change in velocity is negative, so the acceleration calculated from a = (∆v)/t comes out negative; a deceleration of 4 m/s² is the same thing as an acceleration of -4 m/s².

An everyday acceleration is estimated by choosing sensible values for a change in velocity and the time it takes, then dividing. A family car pulling away from traffic lights might reach about 13 m/s in about 6 s, giving roughly 2 m/s²; a cyclist starting off might manage about 1 m/s². Most everyday accelerations are of the order of a few m/s², well below the 9.8 m/s² of free fall.

The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph: the change in velocity (in m/s) divided by the change in time (in s) gives an acceleration in m/s². A horizontal line means constant velocity and therefore zero acceleration; a downward slope means the object is decelerating.

concepts.term: Distance from the area under a velocity-time graph
concepts.definition: (HT only) The distance travelled by an object (or displacement of an object) can be calculated from the area under a velocity-time graph. For straight-line sections the area is found by splitting the region into rectangles and triangles and adding the areas together.

(HT only) Where a velocity-time graph is curved, the area beneath it is not a simple rectangle or triangle, so the area is measured, when appropriate, by counting squares. The area of one grid square is worked out from the axis scales (for example 1 m/s × 1 s = 1 m), whole squares under the line are counted, and part-squares of more than half are counted as whole ones.

The following equation applies to uniform acceleration: (final velocity)² - (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance, written in symbols as v² - u² = 2 a s, where final velocity, v, and initial velocity, u, are in metres per second, m/s; acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s²; and distance, s, is in metres, m. This equation is provided in the exam rather than recalled. It links velocities to a distance without needing the time, and v² - u² must be worked out by squaring each velocity first.

Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s². The word 'any' matters: the acceleration is the same whatever the mass of the object, provided it is falling freely, that is with no significant resistive force acting.

An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. As its speed increases, the resistive force from the fluid increases, so the resultant force and therefore the acceleration decrease. Eventually the resultant force will be zero and the object will move at its terminal velocity - a constant velocity, not a stop.

(Physics only) A velocity-time graph for an object reaching terminal velocity starts steep, becomes progressively less steep as the resistive force grows, and finally levels off to a horizontal line at the terminal velocity. The changing motion is interpreted in terms of the forces: the steep start is where weight greatly exceeds the resistive force, the curve is where the resultant force is falling, and the horizontal line is where weight and the resistive force are balanced so the resultant force is zero.

misconceptions.question: A student walks 30 m north along a corridor and then walks 30 m back. What is the displacement?
misconceptions.correct: Zero. The finish point is the start point, so the straight line from start to finish has zero length.
misconceptions.misconception: Distance and displacement are two words for the same thing, so the displacement must be 60 m as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are lengths measured in metres, and in the simplest examples met first - a straight walk from A to B - the two numbers really are equal. Students generalise from those examples and never meet a case where the two differ until much later.
misconceptions.correction: Distance is how far an object moves along its whole path; displacement is measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point and includes direction. On an out-and-back journey the distance is 60 m but the displacement is zero.

misconceptions.question: A hiker finishes 12 km from where she started. Is '12 km' a complete statement of her displacement?
misconceptions.correct: No. A displacement must be given as a magnitude and a direction, for example 12 km due north.
misconceptions.misconception: The direction is extra detail. As long as I have written the number and the unit, I have given the displacement.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every quantity students have met before - mass, time, distance, energy - is complete once a number and a unit are written down, so writing a direction feels like optional commentary rather than part of the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Displacement is a vector quantity: it includes both the distance measured in a straight line from start to finish and the direction of that straight line. Leaving the direction out leaves the displacement only half stated.

misconceptions.question: Is it correct to say a car has a velocity of 25 m/s?
misconceptions.correct: Not on its own. Speed is 25 m/s; velocity needs a direction too, for example 25 m/s due east.
misconceptions.misconception: Speed and velocity are just two words for the same idea - velocity is the posh word teachers use for speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English the two words are interchangeable, and in most calculations students do the numbers are identical. Nothing in the arithmetic forces them apart, so the distinction looks like vocabulary rather than physics.
misconceptions.correction: The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction. Speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector; an object can hold a constant speed while its velocity changes, which is impossible if the two mean the same thing.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist rides 9 km due east then 4 km due west back along the same road. What is her displacement?
misconceptions.correct: 5 km due east: the straight line from start point to finish point is 5 km long and points east.
misconceptions.misconception: She was heading west at the end, so the displacement must be 5 km due west.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch on to the most recent piece of information - the direction of travel at the finish - because that is what they were last thinking about, and because 'displacement' sounds like it describes the motion rather than the position.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of a displacement is the direction of the straight line drawn from the start point to the finish point, not the direction the object was travelling in at the end. The cyclist finishes 5 km east of where she began.

misconceptions.question: A runner covers 800 m at 8 m/s and then 1000 m at 20 m/s. What is his average speed?
misconceptions.correct: 12 m/s: the total distance, 1800 m, divided by the total time, 150 s.
misconceptions.misconception: Just average the two speeds: (8 + 20)/2 = 14 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Average' in maths lessons almost always means 'add them up and divide by how many', and that rule works whenever the two parts take equal times - which is exactly the case teachers use first.
misconceptions.correction: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Averaging the speeds only gives the same answer when equal times are spent at each speed; here more time is spent at the slower speed, so the true average, 12 m/s, is below the mean of 14 m/s.

misconceptions.question: A car journey includes a fast motorway section at 30 m/s. Is 30 m/s the average speed for the journey?
misconceptions.correct: No. The average speed is the total distance for the whole journey divided by the total time, including slow sections and stops.
misconceptions.misconception: Take the speed of the main part of the journey - the bit where the car was really travelling - and use that as the average.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of stops and slow sections as interruptions to the journey rather than as part of it, so they exclude them, and picking one representative speed feels more concrete than combining totals.
misconceptions.correction: Every second counts towards the total time, including time spent stationary. The average speed of the whole journey is total distance divided by total time, which is always lower than the fastest section.

misconceptions.question: A distance-time graph passes through the origin and the point (20 s, 100 m). What is the speed?
misconceptions.correct: 5 m/s: the gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time, 100 m / 20 s.
misconceptions.misconception: Speed is time divided by distance, so 20/100 = 0.2 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that speed is 'something over something' but not which way round, and 0.2 looks as reasonable an answer as 5 when there is no sense of what the number should be.
misconceptions.correction: s = v t rearranges to v = s/t: distance divided by time. The unit is the check - metres per second means metres divided by seconds, so the distance must be on top.

misconceptions.question: A car covers 100 m in 20 s. What is its speed?
misconceptions.correct: 5 m/s, found by dividing the distance by the time.
misconceptions.misconception: The equation is distance = speed × time, so to get speed I multiply the numbers: 100 × 20 = 2000 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The version of the equation students memorise contains a multiplication sign, so they reach for multiplication whichever quantity they are asked for, and a triangle mnemonic used without understanding makes it easy to pick the wrong operation.
misconceptions.correction: Multiplication only gives the distance. Rearranging distance travelled = speed × time gives speed = distance / time; multiplying two of the quantities together can never produce the third one on the left of the equation.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist travels at 6 m/s for 4 minutes. How far does she travel?
misconceptions.correct: 1440 m: 4 minutes is 240 s, and 6 × 240 = 1440.
misconceptions.misconception: Put the numbers straight into s = v t: 6 × 4 = 24 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation contains the symbol t and the question contains a time, so students substitute what they are given without checking the unit. The specification's unit list is treated as a formality rather than a condition of use.
misconceptions.correction: In s = v t the time t must be in seconds, s, because the speed is in metres per second. Four minutes is 240 s, so the distance is 1440 m - sixty times the answer obtained by substituting 4.

misconceptions.question: An echo returns from a cliff 5.0 s after a shout. Using 330 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
misconceptions.correct: 825 m. The sound travels 1650 m in total, but that is to the cliff and back, so the cliff is half that away.
misconceptions.misconception: The sound travelled for 5.0 s at 330 m/s, so the cliff must be 1650 m away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: s = v t is applied faithfully and gives a correct distance - it is just the distance travelled by the sound, not the distance to the cliff. Nothing in the arithmetic signals that the journey was there and back.
misconceptions.correction: s = v t gives the total path length of the sound, 1650 m. That path is out to the cliff and back again, so the distance to the cliff is 1650/2 = 825 m.

misconceptions.question: Is the speed of sound always 330 m/s?
misconceptions.correct: No. 330 m/s is a typical value for the speed of sound in air; the speed of sound varies.
misconceptions.misconception: 330 m/s is a constant of nature, like the speed of light - sound always travels at exactly that speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The figure is printed in textbooks and data sheets with no qualification, which makes it look like a fixed constant, and students meet it only ever in air at ordinary temperatures.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the speed of sound varies, and gives 330 m/s only as a typical value for air. Sound travels at very different speeds in water and in solids.

misconceptions.question: A pedestrian is timed walking at 1.2 m/s. Is the specification's typical value of 1.5 m/s wrong?
misconceptions.correct: No. 1.5 m/s is a typical value for estimating; real walking speeds vary from person to person.
misconceptions.misconception: The typical values are the true values, so any speed I meet must be 1.5, 3 or 6 m/s - anything else means the measurement is wrong.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Values that have to be learnt for an exam feel like fixed facts of the same kind as the number of protons in carbon, so students treat approximate benchmarks as exact constants and distrust real data that disagrees.
misconceptions.correction: The specification writes these values with an approximation sign and states plainly that the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled. They are benchmarks for estimating, not exact values.

misconceptions.question: A student writes that a typical cycling speed is 15 m/s and a typical car speed is 6 m/s. What is wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The values have been swapped and inflated: cycling is about 6 m/s and a car about 25 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The typical speed values are a list of numbers to learn; it does not much matter which one goes with which activity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The values are usually revised as a bare list, so they are stored as numbers rather than as facts about particular activities, and the cost of pairing them wrongly is invisible until a calculation gives an absurd answer.
misconceptions.correction: Each value belongs to a particular activity: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s, with a car about 25 m/s, a train about 55 m/s and an aeroplane about 250 m/s. Checking whether an answer is sensible depends on the pairing being right.

misconceptions.question: Two equally fit walkers cover the same route, one on a flat pavement and one over rough moorland. Will their speeds match?
misconceptions.correct: No. Terrain is one of the factors the specification lists, and rough ground reduces walking speed.
misconceptions.misconception: How fast you can walk, run or cycle depends on how fit you are and nothing else.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fitness is the factor students hear about constantly in PE and in advertising, and it is the only one that feels like it belongs to the person rather than the situation.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists several factors: age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled. Terrain and distance belong to the journey, not the person, and both change the speed that can be achieved.

misconceptions.question: Can a runner keep up the same speed over 10 km as over 100 m?
misconceptions.correct: No. Distance travelled is one of the listed factors: the speed that can be sustained falls as the distance rises.
misconceptions.misconception: Distance cannot affect speed - the distance is what you work out from the speed, so it cannot be a cause of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the equation s = v t distance is an output, so students conclude it cannot also be an influence, confusing a mathematical relationship with a physical cause.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists distance travelled among the factors affecting the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle. A sprint speed simply cannot be sustained over a long distance.

misconceptions.question: A ball moves at 4 m/s due south. What is its velocity?
misconceptions.correct: 4 m/s due south - the velocity is the speed together with the direction.
misconceptions.misconception: The speed is 4 m/s and the velocity is 'due south' - the number is the speed and the direction is the velocity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being told repeatedly that 'velocity has direction' is compressed to 'velocity is direction', especially as the direction is the only visible difference between the two words.
misconceptions.correction: The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction. A velocity is a magnitude and a direction together; the direction on its own is not a velocity and has no unit.

misconceptions.question: (HT only) A car drives round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Is its velocity constant?
misconceptions.correct: No. The speed is constant but the direction of motion changes continuously, so the velocity is changing.
misconceptions.misconception: The speedometer reads a steady 8 m/s, so nothing about the motion is changing - the velocity is constant too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge 'changing' by what a speedometer would show, and a speedometer measures speed only. Direction change is not felt as change because the number stays put.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is a vector, so it changes if either the magnitude or the direction changes. Motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity, because the direction of travel is different at every point around the circle.

misconceptions.question: A distance-time graph has a horizontal section. What is the object doing during it?
misconceptions.correct: It is stationary: time passes but the distance does not change.
misconceptions.misconception: A flat line means nothing is changing about the motion, so the object is moving along at a steady speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Flat line means steady' is a correct reading of a velocity-time graph, and students apply it to whichever graph is in front of them without checking what is on the vertical axis.
misconceptions.correction: On a distance-time graph the vertical axis is distance. If the line is horizontal, the distance is not increasing, so the object is not moving. Steady speed appears as a straight line with a constant non-zero slope.

misconceptions.question: A distance-time graph is a straight sloping line. Is the object accelerating?
misconceptions.correct: No. A constant gradient means a constant speed, so the object is not accelerating.
misconceptions.misconception: The line is going up, so the object is going faster and faster - a rising line means speeding up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the height of the line rather than its slope: distance keeps increasing, which they interpret as 'more and more motion'. The idea that speed is the slope, not the value, has to displace a strong visual instinct.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is read from the gradient of a distance-time graph, not from the height of the line. A constant gradient is constant speed; speeding up shows as a curve whose gradient increases.

misconceptions.question: A distance-time graph for a cyclist rises steeply. Does this mean she is going up a hill?
misconceptions.correct: No. The steep line means a high speed; the graph is not a picture of the route.
misconceptions.misconception: The shape of the line shows the shape of the journey - a steep line is a steep hill and a flat line is flat ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Axes are ignored and the line is read as a sketch of the landscape, which is how most pictures students meet work. The label 'distance' on the vertical axis is not connected to what the height of the line means.
misconceptions.correction: A distance-time graph plots distance against time, not height against position. A steep line means a large distance covered in a short time, which is a high speed; going up a hill would in fact make the line less steep.

misconceptions.question: (HT only) A distance-time graph curves upwards. How is the speed at t = 6 s found?
misconceptions.correct: Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 6 s and measure the gradient of that tangent.
misconceptions.misconception: Join the origin to the point on the curve at t = 6 s and find the gradient of that straight line.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The origin-to-point line is easy to draw and gives a defensible-looking number, and for a straight-line graph it would be right. Students do not distinguish the average speed so far from the speed at that instant.
misconceptions.correction: The gradient of the line from the origin gives the average speed over the whole 6 s, not the speed at 6 s. For an accelerating object the speed at a particular time is found by drawing a tangent at that time and measuring its gradient.

misconceptions.question: A car speeds up from 6 m/s to 30 m/s in 8.0 s. What is its acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 m/s²: the change in velocity is 30 - 6 = 24 m/s, and 24/8 = 3.0.
misconceptions.misconception: Acceleration is velocity divided by time, so it is 30/8 = 3.75 m/s².
misconceptions.whyItArises: The initial velocity looks like background information, and in every first example the object starts from rest, where the final velocity and the change in velocity happen to be equal. The shortcut then survives into cases where it fails.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken). The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity; using the final velocity alone is only correct when the object starts from rest.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 4.0 s. What is her acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: -2.0 m/s². The change in velocity is 4 - 12 = -8 m/s, so the acceleration is negative.
misconceptions.misconception: She is slowing down, so I subtract the smaller from the larger to keep it positive: the acceleration is 2.0 m/s².
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught to avoid negative answers in earlier maths, and 'deceleration of 2 m/s²' is a perfectly good phrase, so the minus sign is discarded as untidy rather than recognised as information.
misconceptions.correction: An object that slows down is decelerating, and change in velocity = final - initial gives a negative value. The acceleration is -2.0 m/s², which may also be described as a deceleration of 2.0 m/s²; the sign must not simply be dropped when 'acceleration' is asked for.

misconceptions.question: A lift accelerates at 1.2. What unit belongs with this number?
misconceptions.correct: m/s² - metres per second squared, the unit of acceleration given in the specification.
misconceptions.misconception: Acceleration is about how fast something is going, so it is measured in m/s like speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acceleration is introduced through examples full of speeds in m/s, and the squared second has no everyday meaning that students can picture, so it is treated as a decoration on the familiar unit.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is a change of velocity per second, so its unit is (m/s) per second, written m/s². Using m/s would mean the quantity was a velocity, not an acceleration.

misconceptions.question: In the unit m/s², what is being squared?
misconceptions.correct: The second. The unit is metres per second per second - the metres are not squared.
misconceptions.misconception: The whole thing is squared, or the metres are - m/s² is really something like square metres per second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The superscript sits at the end of the unit, so it looks as if it applies to everything before it, and students have met m² for area far more often than s² for anything.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration = (change in velocity in m/s)/(time in s), so the unit is (m/s)/s = m/s². Only the time unit is squared; m²/s would be an area per second and has nothing to do with acceleration.

misconceptions.question: Estimate the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights.
misconceptions.correct: About 2 m/s² - roughly 13 m/s reached in roughly 6 s.
misconceptions.misconception: Accelerations are about 10 m/s², because that is the acceleration due to gravity and it is the value we always use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 9.8 m/s² is the only acceleration students ever see a number for, so it becomes the mental yardstick for all accelerations, and cars feel fast in everyday terms.
misconceptions.correction: Everyday accelerations are estimated from a realistic change in velocity and a realistic time. A car reaching about 13 m/s in about 6 s accelerates at roughly 2 m/s², several times smaller than the 9.8 m/s² of free fall.

misconceptions.question: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph give?
misconceptions.correct: The acceleration of the object.
misconceptions.misconception: The gradient gives the distance travelled, because the steeper the line the further the object has gone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gradient and area are both taught as things you extract from a velocity-time graph, and with two techniques and two quantities the pairing is a coin toss for a student who has learnt the methods but not the reasoning.
misconceptions.correction: The gradient is a change in velocity divided by a change in time, which is exactly the definition of acceleration and gives units of m/s². Distance comes from the area under the line, whose units are (m/s) × s = m.

misconceptions.question: On a velocity-time graph, does the gradient give the speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. On a velocity-time graph the gradient gives the acceleration; speed is read directly off the vertical axis.
misconceptions.misconception: The gradient of a motion graph always tells you the speed - that is what gradients are for.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first graph students meet is the distance-time graph, where the gradient really is the speed. That rule is stored as a fact about gradients rather than as a fact about that particular pair of axes.
misconceptions.correction: What a gradient means depends on the axes. On a distance-time graph it is distance/time, a speed; on a velocity-time graph it is velocity/time, an acceleration. On a velocity-time graph the speed is simply the height of the line.

misconceptions.question: (HT only) What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
misconceptions.correct: The distance travelled by the object, or its displacement.
misconceptions.misconception: The area under the line gives the acceleration - a bigger area means a bigger acceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a velocity-time graph yields acceleration and distance, and remember both words without securing which technique produces which, so the two are attached the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Area is height × width, that is velocity × time, which has units of (m/s) × s = m - a distance. Acceleration comes from the gradient, not the area.

misconceptions.question: (HT only) A student says the area under a velocity-time graph gives the average speed. Is that right?
misconceptions.correct: No. The area gives the distance travelled; the average speed would be that distance divided by the total time.
misconceptions.misconception: You are adding up all the velocities under the line, so the area must be the average of them - the average speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Adding up the velocities' is a reasonable-sounding description of an area under a velocity axis, and it lands on the familiar idea of averaging rather than on the unfamiliar idea of a product.
misconceptions.correction: An area multiplies velocity by time, it does not average velocities, and the units confirm it: (m/s) × s = m. The area gives distance travelled or displacement; an average speed would then be found by dividing that distance by the total time.

misconceptions.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m/s² over 100 m. What is its final velocity?
misconceptions.correct: 20 m/s. 2 a s = 400, so v² = 400 and v is the square root, 20 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: 2 × 2.0 × 100 = 400, so the final velocity is 400 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The arithmetic finishes at 400 and the answer line is waiting, so the last step is skipped. Because the equation is provided on the exam sheet, students substitute into it mechanically without tracking that the subject is v².
misconceptions.correction: The equation is v² - u² = 2 a s, so the calculation gives v², not v. After finding v² = 400 (m/s)² the square root must be taken, giving v = 20 m/s. A quick sanity check helps: 400 m/s is faster than the speed of sound.

misconceptions.question: A motorbike speeds up from 15 m/s to 25 m/s at 2.0 m/s². What distance does it cover?
misconceptions.misconception: Use v² = 2 a s, so 625 = 4.0 × s and the distance is about 156 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every worked example starts from rest, where u = 0 and the u² term genuinely disappears. Students remember the simplified version of the equation rather than the full one and apply it to objects that are already moving.
misconceptions.correction: The u² term can only be dropped when the object starts from rest. Here the motorbike is already travelling at 15 m/s, so v² - u² = 625 - 225 = 400, giving a distance of 100 m rather than 156 m.

misconceptions.question: In v² - u² = 2 a s with u = 15 m/s and v = 25 m/s, what is the value of v² - u²?
misconceptions.correct: 400 (m/s)²: square each velocity first, 625 - 225 = 400.
misconceptions.misconception: Subtract first and then square: (25 - 15)² = 10² = 100.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see two velocities and a subtraction and reach for the change in velocity, which is what every other equation in the topic uses. Squaring the bracket afterwards feels like the same operation in a different order.
misconceptions.correction: v² - u² is the difference of the squares, not the square of the difference: each velocity must be squared before subtracting. Here 625 - 225 = 400, whereas (25 - 15)² gives 100 and a distance four times too small.

misconceptions.question: A heavy ball and a light ball are dropped together and fall freely. Which has the greater acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. Any object falling freely near the Earth's surface has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s².
misconceptions.misconception: The heavier ball accelerates more, because gravity pulls harder on a bigger mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is true that a greater mass has a greater weight, and students stop there. Everyday experience with feathers and paper, where air resistance dominates, appears to confirm it.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s². A greater mass does have a greater weight, but it also needs a greater force to accelerate it, and the two effects cancel exactly.

misconceptions.question: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity. What is happening to her motion?
misconceptions.correct: She continues to fall, at a constant velocity, because the resultant force on her is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: The forces are balanced, so she stops falling and hangs still in the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over the idea that a zero resultant force means no motion, because the balanced-forces examples they meet first are stationary objects on tables and floors.
misconceptions.correction: A zero resultant force means no change in velocity, not no velocity. Eventually the resultant force will be zero and the object will move at its terminal velocity - moving steadily, not stopping.

misconceptions.question: At terminal velocity, what forces act on a falling skydiver?
misconceptions.correct: Weight downwards and air resistance upwards, equal in size, so the resultant force is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: There are no forces on her any more - that is why she has stopped accelerating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Resultant force is zero' is read as 'force is zero'. The two individual forces become invisible once their effects cancel, and nothing in the motion reveals them.
misconceptions.correction: The forces do not disappear; they balance. Weight still acts downwards and the air resistance has grown until it is equal and opposite, so the resultant force - the sum of the two - is zero while both forces remain large.

misconceptions.question: As a skydiver falls faster before terminal velocity, what happens to her weight?
misconceptions.correct: It stays the same. Her weight is unchanged; it is the air resistance that increases.
misconceptions.misconception: The air resistance pushes up against her weight, so her weight gets smaller as she speeds up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students describe the shrinking resultant force in terms of the quantity they can name, and 'feeling lighter' is a real everyday sensation, so weight is imagined to be used up by the opposing force.
misconceptions.correction: Weight depends on mass and gravitational field strength, neither of which changes during the fall. It is the air resistance that increases with speed, which is why the resultant force and the acceleration both fall to zero.

misconceptions.question: A skydiver falls through the air for a long time. Is her acceleration 9.8 m/s² all the way down?
misconceptions.correct: No. It starts at about 9.8 m/s² and falls towards zero as the air resistance builds up.
misconceptions.misconception: Gravity does not change during the fall, so the acceleration stays at 9.8 m/s² the whole way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The value 9.8 m/s² is learnt as a property of the Earth rather than as the acceleration of an object in free fall, so it seems to apply to anything falling anywhere, whatever else is acting.
misconceptions.correction: 9.8 m/s² applies to an object falling freely, that is with no significant resistive force. An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates at about that rate, but as its speed rises the resistive force grows, the resultant force falls, and the acceleration decreases to zero at terminal velocity.

mcqs.stem: A student walks 30 m due north along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to where she started. What are the distance she has travelled and her displacement?

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement 0 m.
options.rationale: Distance is the whole path walked, 30 m + 30 m = 60 m. The straight line from start point to finish point has zero length, so the displacement is zero.

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement 60 m.
options.rationale: The student treats the two quantities as the same thing and quotes the path length twice.

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement 30 m.
options.rationale: The student takes the displacement to be how far from the start she got at the furthest point, ignoring the return journey.

options.text: Distance 30 m; displacement 30 m south.
options.rationale: The student uses the final leg only, taking its length as the distance and its direction as the direction of the displacement.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a correctly stated displacement?

options.text: A displacement of 12 m along the path walked.
options.rationale: Measuring along the path is how distance is found; displacement is measured in a straight line from start to finish.

options.text: A displacement of 12 m, which is all needed.
options.rationale: The student treats the direction as optional extra detail rather than part of the quantity.

options.text: A displacement of 12 metres per second north.
options.rationale: The direction is there but the unit is one of velocity, not displacement; the student has confused the vector pair.

options.text: A displacement of 12 m due north of the start.
options.rationale: A displacement needs both a magnitude and the direction of the straight line from start point to finish point, and both are given here.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist rides 9 km due east along a straight road, then turns round and rides 4 km due west along the same road. What is her displacement from her start point?

options.text: 13 km due east
options.rationale: The student adds the two legs, which gives the distance travelled, not the displacement.

options.text: 5 km due west
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the direction is taken from the last leg of the ride instead of from the start-to-finish line.

options.text: 4 km due west
options.rationale: The student quotes the return leg on its own, treating the outward ride as cancelled and forgotten.

options.text: 5 km due east
options.rationale: The straight line from start point to finish point is 9 km - 4 km = 5 km long, and the finish point lies east of the start.

mcqs.stem: A student writes: 'distance and speed are vectors; displacement and velocity are scalars.' What correction is needed?

options.text: Swap them: displacement and velocity are the vectors.
options.rationale: Displacement and velocity both include a direction, so both are vectors; distance and speed have magnitude only and are scalars.

options.text: No correction: the classification given is correct.
options.rationale: A student who treats the words as interchangeable sees no reason why one label should be better than another.

options.text: Only speed is wrong; it is a vector quantity too.
options.rationale: A student who thinks direction is the whole of velocity looks for direction words, decides speed carries one too, and patches only that.

options.text: Only distance is wrong; it is a scalar quantity.
options.rationale: A half correction: the student spots that distance has no direction but leaves the other three labels untouched.

mcqs.stem: Which set of typical speeds matches the values given in the specification?

options.text: walking 3 m/s, running 6 m/s, cycling 15 m/s
options.rationale: The values have been shifted along by one activity, a common result of learning them as a bare list of numbers.

options.text: walking 0.5 m/s, running 1.5 m/s, cycling 3 m/s
options.rationale: Every value is halved; the student has anchored on remembered figures without checking them against experience.

options.text: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s
options.rationale: These are the typical values the specification states for a person walking, running and cycling.

options.text: walking 1.5 m/s, running 6 m/s, cycling 15 m/s
options.rationale: Walking is right but running and cycling have been doubled, exaggerating how much faster each activity is.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist travels for 4 minutes at the typical cycling speed given in the specification. How far does she travel?

options.rationale: Typical cycling speed is 6 m/s and 4 minutes is 240 s, so s = v t = 6 × 240 = 1440 m.
The time has been substituted as 4 rather than converted to 240 s, making the answer sixty times too small.
The time is converted correctly but the walking value of 1.5 m/s has been used instead of the cycling value.
The running value of 3 m/s has been used in place of the cycling value of 6 m/s.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the speed of sound is correct?

options.text: It is exactly 330 m/s in air and never varies at all.
options.rationale: The figure is treated as a fixed constant of nature because it is always quoted without qualification.

options.text: It varies, but only between about 3 m/s and 6 m/s.
options.rationale: The student anchors on the only typical speeds recalled - running and cycling - and assumes all typical values are of that size.

options.text: A typical value is 330 m/s, and the actual value varies.
options.rationale: The specification gives 330 m/s as a typical value for the speed of sound in air and states that the speed of sound varies.

options.text: It is the same in air, water and steel: about 330 m/s.
options.rationale: The value for air is generalised to every material, when in fact sound travels far faster in liquids and solids.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the factors the specification names as affecting the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle?

options.text: Only fitness and age; terrain does not matter
options.rationale: The student keeps the factors that belong to the person and discards the one that belongs to the ground.

options.text: Age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled
options.rationale: These are exactly the four factors listed in the specification.

options.text: Age, terrain and fitness, but not the distance
options.rationale: Distance is dropped because it is seen as something calculated from speed rather than something that limits it.

options.text: Only the terrain the person is moving over
options.rationale: One correct factor is selected and the others discarded, as though a single cause had to be chosen.

mcqs.stem: A train travels at a constant speed of 45 m/s for 3.0 minutes. What distance does it travel?

options.rationale: The time is substituted as 3 rather than 180 s, so the answer is sixty times too small.
Three minutes is 180 s, so s = v t = 45 × 180 = 8100 m.
The student divides instead of multiplying, using 45/3 without noticing that distance is required.
The arithmetic is right but the unit is wrong; the student assumes a long journey must be quoted in kilometres.

mcqs.stem: A walker shouts at a cliff and hears the echo 5.0 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, how far away is the cliff?

options.rationale: s = v t is applied correctly but the answer is the total path of the sound, not the distance to the cliff.
The sound travels s = v t = 330 × 5.0 = 1650 m, but that is to the cliff and back, so the cliff is 1650/2 = 825 m away.
The student divides the speed by the time instead of multiplying, giving a quantity that is not a distance at all.
The student realises the sound made a return journey but doubles the distance instead of halving it.

mcqs.stem: A runner covers 800 m in 100 s, then a further 1000 m in 50 s. What is his average speed for the whole run?

options.text: 12 m/s
options.rationale: Average speed is total distance divided by total time: 1800 m / 150 s = 12 m/s.

options.text: 14 m/s
options.rationale: The two speeds, 8 m/s and 20 m/s, are averaged; this is only valid if equal times are spent at each speed.

options.text: 8 m/s
options.rationale: The speed of the first section alone is quoted as though it represented the whole run.

options.text: 20 m/s
options.rationale: The fastest section is quoted, which is the maximum speed reached rather than the average.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to find the average speed of a trolley running down a ramp. Which method is correct?

options.text: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then divide time by distance.
options.rationale: The division is the wrong way round; the unit m/s shows that metres must be on top.

options.text: Measure the distance and the time for the fastest part of the ramp only.
options.rationale: Timing one selected section gives the speed of that section, not the average speed of the whole run.

options.text: Measure the distance travelled and multiply it by the time taken to move.
options.rationale: Multiplying distance by time gives a quantity with units of metre-seconds, which is not a speed.

options.text: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then divide distance by time.
options.rationale: Speed is found from measured values of distance and time, with the distance in metres and the time in seconds.

mcqs.stem: Which statement defines velocity?

options.text: The distance an object moves each second.
options.rationale: This defines speed, which a student who treats the two words as synonyms will offer for either.

options.text: The rate at which an object changes speed.
options.rationale: This describes acceleration; the student has moved one step along the chain of motion quantities.

options.text: The speed of an object in a given direction.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition; it makes velocity a vector quantity.

options.text: The direction in which the object is moving.
options.rationale: 'Velocity has direction' is compressed into 'velocity is direction', leaving a quantity with no magnitude or unit.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A car drives round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Which statement about its motion is correct?

options.text: Both its speed and its velocity are constant here.
options.rationale: The student judges 'changing' by what a speedometer would show, and a speedometer reads speed only.

options.text: Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing.
options.rationale: The two labels are swapped by a student for whom the words are interchangeable.

options.text: Its speed is constant but its velocity is changing.
options.rationale: The magnitude of the motion is unchanged, but the direction of travel changes continuously, and velocity is a vector.

options.text: Its speed and its velocity are both changing here.
options.rationale: The student correctly sees that something is changing but attributes it to the speed as well as the direction.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) Why does an object moving in a circle at constant speed have a changing velocity?

options.text: Its speed must be changing even though it looks constant.
options.rationale: The student assumes velocity can only change if the speed changes, so invents a hidden change of speed.

options.text: The distance it moves each second keeps on increasing.
options.rationale: Changing velocity is read as covering more ground each second, which would mean the speed was not constant.

options.text: Velocity always changes whenever an object is moving.
options.rationale: An overgeneralisation: an object moving in a straight line at steady speed has a constant velocity.

options.text: Its direction of motion changes continuously as it moves.
options.rationale: Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction alone is a change of velocity even when the speed is fixed.

mcqs.stem: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line show?

options.text: The object is not moving at all.
options.rationale: Time passes but the distance does not change, so the object is stationary.

options.text: The object moves at a steady speed.
options.rationale: 'Flat means steady' is the correct reading of a velocity-time graph, applied to the wrong axes.

options.text: The object is returning to the start.
options.rationale: Returning towards the start would show as a line sloping downwards, not a horizontal one.

options.text: The object is speeding up steadily.
options.rationale: The student reads the height of the line rather than its gradient and sees continuing motion.

mcqs.stem: A distance-time graph is a straight line through the origin and through the point (20 s, 100 m). What is the speed of the object?

options.rationale: Time has been divided by distance; the unit m/s shows the division is the wrong way round.
The two coordinates have been multiplied, as in distance = speed × time, instead of divided.

options.text: 5 m/s
options.rationale: Speed is the gradient: change in distance divided by change in time, 100 m / 20 s = 5 m/s.
The distance value is read straight off the axis and given a speed unit, with no gradient calculated.

mcqs.stem: A distance-time graph for a car is a curve that becomes steeper as time goes on. What does this show?

options.text: The car travels at a steady speed here.
options.rationale: The student reads the rising line as motion continuing rather than reading its changing slope.

options.text: The car is climbing a hill as it goes.
options.rationale: The line is read as a picture of the route instead of as a plot of distance against time.

options.text: The car's speed is increasing with time.
options.rationale: Speed is the gradient, so a gradient that increases means the car is speeding up.

options.text: The car's speed is decreasing with time.
options.rationale: The steepening is interpreted backwards; a curve that flattens out would show a falling speed.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A distance-time graph for an accelerating cyclist is a curve. How is the cyclist's speed at t = 6 s found?

options.text: Divide the distance shown at t = 6 s by the time of 6 s.
options.rationale: This gives the average speed over the whole 6 s, which for an accelerating object is less than the speed at 6 s.

options.text: Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 6 s and find its gradient.
options.rationale: The gradient of the tangent at that point gives the speed at that instant.

options.text: Find the gradient of the straight line from 0 s to 6 s.
options.rationale: Joining the origin to the point gives the same average value as dividing distance by time, not the instantaneous speed.

options.text: Read the value off the distance axis at the time t = 6 s.
options.rationale: This gives a distance in metres, not a speed; no gradient has been taken at all.

mcqs.stem: A car speeds up uniformly from 6.0 m/s to 30 m/s in 8.0 s. What is its average acceleration?

options.rationale: The final velocity is divided by the time, ignoring the fact that the car was already moving at 6.0 m/s.

options.text: 4.5 m/s²
options.rationale: The two velocities are added rather than subtracted, giving 36/8.0.

options.text: 3.0 m/s²
options.rationale: The change in velocity is 30 - 6.0 = 24 m/s, so a = 24/8.0 = 3.0 m/s².
The time is divided by the change in velocity, so the division is inverted.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist slows uniformly from 12 m/s to 4.0 m/s in 4.0 s. What is her acceleration?

options.text: 2.0 m/s²
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the minus sign has been dropped, so the answer describes speeding up.
The change in velocity is 4.0 - 12 = -8.0 m/s, so a = -8.0/4.0 = -2.0 m/s², a deceleration of 2.0 m/s².
The two velocities are added instead of subtracted, giving -16/4.0.
The initial velocity is divided by the time instead of the change in velocity being used.

mcqs.stem: A student writes 'the acceleration of the lift is 1.2 m/s'. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; acceleration is measured in m/s.
options.rationale: Acceleration is taken to be a kind of speed, so the speed unit is accepted for it.

options.text: Acceleration should be given in m²/s, not in m/s.
options.rationale: The square is attached to the metres rather than to the seconds, giving an area per second.

options.text: Acceleration is measured in m/s², not in m/s.
options.rationale: Acceleration is a change of velocity per second, so its unit is (m/s) per second, written m/s².

options.text: Acceleration should be given in seconds per metre.
options.rationale: The unit is inverted, which would correspond to dividing time by velocity rather than the reverse.

mcqs.stem: A family car pulls away from traffic lights and reaches about 13 m/s in about 6 s. Which is the best estimate of its acceleration?

options.text: About 2 m/s²
options.rationale: 13 m/s divided by 6 s is roughly 2 m/s², a realistic value for an everyday car.

options.text: About 10 m/s²
options.rationale: The only acceleration the student can put a number to is that of free fall, so it is used for everything.

options.text: About 80 m/s²
options.rationale: The velocity and time have been multiplied instead of divided.

options.text: About 0.5 m/s²
options.rationale: The time has been divided by the velocity, inverting the calculation.

mcqs.stem: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?

options.text: The distance the object travels.
options.rationale: Gradient and area are swapped; distance comes from the area beneath the line.

options.text: The acceleration of the object.
options.rationale: The gradient is a change in velocity divided by a change in time, which gives m/s² - an acceleration.

options.text: The speed of the object at a time.
options.rationale: The rule for distance-time graphs is carried over; on this graph the speed is the height of the line.

options.text: The average velocity of the object.
options.rationale: An average velocity would come from the whole line's height, not from its slope.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?

options.text: The acceleration of the object here.
options.rationale: Area and gradient are swapped; acceleration is found from the slope of the line.

options.text: The average speed of the object.
options.rationale: The area is imagined as an average of the velocities rather than as a product of velocity and time.

options.text: The final velocity of the object.
options.rationale: The final velocity is read directly off the vertical axis at the end of the line, not from an area.

options.text: The distance travelled by the object.
options.rationale: Area is velocity multiplied by time, with units (m/s) × s = m, so it gives distance travelled or displacement.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A velocity-time graph for a falling object is a curve. Why is the distance travelled found by counting squares?

options.text: Counting squares gives the gradient of the curved line here.
options.rationale: Squares measure area, not slope; the gradient of a curve is found by drawing a tangent.

options.text: The area under a curved line has no physical meaning.
options.rationale: The area still represents distance travelled; it is only harder to calculate than for straight sections.

options.text: Squares are counted to find the average velocity value.
options.rationale: The area is taken to be an average of the velocities rather than a distance.

options.text: The area under a curve is not a simple rectangle or triangle.
options.rationale: Counting squares measures an area of any shape once the value of one square has been worked out from the axes.

mcqs.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m/s² over a distance of 100 m. What is its final velocity? (v² - u² = 2 a s)

options.text: 20 m/s
options.rationale: v² - u² = 2 × 2.0 × 100 = 400, and with u = 0 this gives v² = 400, so v = 20 m/s.
The calculation is stopped at v², so the square root has not been taken.
The acceleration and distance are multiplied and quoted directly, dropping both the factor of 2 and the square root.

options.text: 14 m/s
options.rationale: The factor of 2 is omitted, giving v² = 200 and a final velocity about 30 per cent too small.

mcqs.stem: A motorbike accelerates uniformly from 15 m/s to 25 m/s with an acceleration of 2.0 m/s². What distance does it travel while doing so? (v² - u² = 2 a s)

options.rationale: The initial velocity is left out, so 625 = 4.0 s is solved instead of 400 = 4.0 s.
The change in velocity is squared, (25 - 15)² = 100, instead of the squares being subtracted.
The change in velocity is divided by the acceleration, which gives a time in seconds, not a distance.

mcqs.stem: A ball is dropped near the Earth's surface and falls freely. What is its acceleration?

options.text: About 9.8 m/s, downwards
options.rationale: The number is right but the unit is that of velocity, so the quantity described is not an acceleration.

options.text: About 9.8 m/s², downwards
options.rationale: Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s².

options.text: It depends on the ball's mass
options.rationale: A greater mass has a greater weight but also needs a greater force to accelerate it; the effects cancel.

options.text: Zero once the ball is falling
options.rationale: Falling freely means the ball is accelerating; zero acceleration would mean a constant velocity.

mcqs.stem: A skydiver falling through the air reaches terminal velocity. Which statement describes what is happening?

options.text: She stops falling, because the forces acting on her are balanced.
options.rationale: Zero resultant force is read as no motion, carried over from stationary balanced-force examples.

options.text: She falls at a constant velocity because the resultant force is zero.
options.rationale: Eventually the resultant force will be zero and the object will move at its terminal velocity.

options.text: She keeps accelerating, but more slowly than she did at the start.
options.rationale: This describes the stage before terminal velocity; at terminal velocity the acceleration has reached zero.

options.text: She has no forces acting on her, so she cannot accelerate at all.
options.rationale: 'Resultant force is zero' is read as 'there are no forces'; weight and air resistance are both still large.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches the velocity-time graph of an object falling through air until it reaches terminal velocity?

options.text: A curve that becomes less steep, then levels off horizontally.
options.rationale: The gradient is the acceleration, which starts near 9.8 m/s² and falls to zero at terminal velocity.

options.text: A straight sloping line of constant gradient for the whole fall.
options.rationale: This would mean the acceleration stayed at 9.8 m/s² throughout, ignoring the growing air resistance.

options.text: A curve that becomes steeper and steeper as the object falls.
options.rationale: An increasing gradient would mean the acceleration was growing, which happens only if resistance falls.

options.text: A line that rises and then falls back down to zero velocity.
options.rationale: Falling back to zero velocity would mean the object stopped in mid-air rather than falling steadily.

mcqs.stem: As a skydiver speeds up during the stage before terminal velocity, what is happening to the forces on her?

options.text: Air resistance increases and her weight decreases as she falls.
options.rationale: Weight is imagined to be used up by the opposing force, but it depends only on mass and gravitational field strength.

options.text: Her weight increases, so the resultant force grows as she falls.
options.rationale: This would give an increasing acceleration, which contradicts the graph levelling off at terminal velocity.

options.text: Both forces stay the same, so her acceleration stays unchanged.
options.rationale: If nothing changed she would keep accelerating at 9.8 m/s² and terminal velocity would never be reached.

options.text: Air resistance increases, so the resultant force gets smaller.
options.rationale: Weight is unchanged while the upward resistive force grows with speed, so the resultant force and the acceleration fall.

mcqs.stem: Why is it usually misleading to say that a car 'travels at 13 m/s' for a whole journey?

options.text: Its speed changes constantly, so 13 m/s is an average.
options.rationale: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant; when people travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.

options.text: Speed cannot be measured accurately enough in a car.
options.rationale: Speed is measured accurately by a speedometer; the problem is the variation, not the measurement.

options.text: 13 m/s is a velocity, so a direction must be given.
options.rationale: The two quantities are treated as the same, so a direction is demanded for a speed.

options.text: Cars can only travel at their typical top speed value.
options.rationale: Typical values are treated as fixed values that every car must have at all times.

mcqs.stem: Which is the most sensible typical speed for a car travelling on a motorway?

options.text: About 6 m/s
options.rationale: The typical cycling value has been used for a car, a sign that the numbers were learnt without their activities.

options.text: About 25 m/s
options.rationale: About 25 m/s is the usual typical value for a car, roughly 90 km/h.

options.text: About 250 m/s
options.rationale: This is the typical speed of a passenger aeroplane, about ten times too fast for a car.

options.text: About 3 m/s
options.rationale: The student assumes every typical speed must be one of the three learnt for people, and picks the running value.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the speed of sound and the speed of the wind is correct?

options.text: Both are fixed constants which never change at all.
options.rationale: Quoted typical values are treated as exact constants that apply in every situation.

options.text: Sound has one fixed speed, but the wind speed varies.
options.rationale: Wind is obviously variable from experience, while 330 m/s looks like a constant of nature.

options.text: Both vary; the figures quoted are only typical values.
options.rationale: The specification states that the speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.

options.text: Wind has one fixed speed, but the speed of sound varies.
options.rationale: The two are the wrong way round; everyday experience alone rules out a fixed wind speed.
